A sharp bound for additive complements

Zihan Zhang Address: School of Mathematical Sciences and LPMC, Nankai University, Tianjin 300071, People’s Republic of China Email address: 2211056@mail.nankai.edu.cn
Abstract.

Let AA and BB be infinite sets of nonnegative integers whose sum contains all sufficiently large integers, and let A⁡(x)A(x) and B⁡(x)B(x) be their counting functions. We give a discrete proof of the sharp implication

lim supx→∞A⁡(x)​B​(x)x<32⟹A⁡(x)​B​(x)−x⟶+∞.\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{A(x)B(x)}{x}<\frac{3}{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad A(x)B(x)-x\longrightarrow+\infty.

The constant 3/23/2 is best possible. Using finite convolution sums, we show that a long gap in one set forces a gap in the other. We then compare the counting functions before and after the gap to obtain the sharp bound.

Key words and phrases: 
Additive complements, counting functions, representation functions, convolution
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 11B13. Secondary 11B34

1. Introduction

We write ℕ0={0,1,2,…}\mathbb{N}_{0}=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}. Two infinite sets A,B⊆ℕ0A,B\subseteq\mathbb{N}_{0} are called additive complements if A+BA+B contains all sufficiently large integers. For real x≥0x\geq 0, put

A⁡(x)=#⁡(A∩[0,x]),B⁡(x)=#⁡(B∩[0,x]).A(x)=\#(A\cap[0,x]),\qquad B(x)=\#(B\cap[0,x]).

Every sufficiently large integer at most xx has a representation using elements at most xx, so A⁡(x)​B​(x)≥x−O⁡(1)A(x)B(x)\geq x-O(1).

Hanani asked whether every pair of infinite additive complements satisfies

lim supx→∞A⁡(x)​B​(x)x>1.\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{A(x)B(x)}{x}>1.

Erdős recorded this question in [3, Problem 12, p. 295]. Danzer [2] answered it negatively by constructing complements for which

(1.1) A⁡(x)​B​(x)x⟶1.\frac{A(x)B(x)}{x}\longrightarrow 1.

Following Ruzsa [8, Section 1], such pairs are called exact additive complements. This terminology refers to the counting functions and does not require unique representations.

Danzer also asked whether (1.1) forces

(1.2) A⁡(x)​B​(x)−x⟶+∞.A(x)B(x)-x\longrightarrow+\infty.

Sárközy and Szemerédi [9] proved that it does. Ruzsa [8, Theorem 1.3] later showed that the excess can grow arbitrarily slowly along a sequence: for any function tending to infinity, there are exact complements whose excess is smaller than that function at arbitrarily large arguments.

Fang and Chen [4] proved (1.2) under the weaker assumption

lim supx→∞A⁡(x)​B​(x)x<54.\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{A(x)B(x)}{x}<\frac{5}{4}.

They replaced 5/45/4 by 3−33-\sqrt{3} in [5, Theorem 1.1], and Yang and Zhao [11, Theorem 1.1] obtained 4/34/3. Chen and Fang [1] also constructed complements with upper limit 3/23/2 and excess equal to 11 at infinitely many integers. Thus 3/23/2 is the largest possible threshold.

A measure-theoretic proof of the sharp 3/23/2 bound was announced by van Doorn, Liu and Tang on 5 August 2026 in the discussion of Erdős Problem 785 [10]. The announcement credits GPT-5.6 Sol with obtaining the proof. The accompanying note takes weak limits of normalized counting measures and uses Gabardo and Lai’s characterization [6] of probability measures whose convolution is Lebesgue measure on [0,1][0,1]. However, they think the proof by is too surprising that they are working now to find a human-generated version. We give a proof of the same conclusion using elementary counting and finite convolutions.

Theorem 1.1.

Let AA and BB be infinite additive complements in ℕ0\mathbb{N}_{0}. If

(1.3) lim supx→∞A⁡(x)​B​(x)x<32,\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{A(x)B(x)}{x}<\frac{3}{2},

then

A⁡(x)​B​(x)−x⟶+∞.A(x)B(x)-x\longrightarrow+\infty.

The proof begins with a standard observation: if the excess stays bounded along a sequence, then every sufficiently large integer has a unique representation as a sum. This reduction was already used in [9, p. 238] and [5, p. 85]. The upper limit assumption then gives consecutive elements x<yx<y of one set with y≥3​x+n0y\geq 3x+n_{0}, where n0n_{0} is fixed.

Our use of these gaps is motivated by the 3/23/2 example of Chen and Fang [1], discussed in Section 6. We prove, uniformly for integers 0≤t≤x0\leq t\leq x, that

A⁡(y+t)=A⁡(x)+A⁡(t)+O⁡(1),A⁡(x)​B​(y+t)=y+O⁡(1).A(y+t)=A(x)+A(t)+O(1),\qquad A(x)B(y+t)=y+O(1).

The first estimate describes how AA grows after the gap; the second controls BB on the same interval. At t=xt=x, they give

A⁡(y+x)​B​(y+x)y+x≥(2−o⁡(1))​yy+x≥32−o⁡(1)\frac{A(y+x)B(y+x)}{y+x}\geq(2-o(1))\frac{y}{y+x}\geq\frac{3}{2}-o(1)

along the sequence of gaps. The reflected convolution identity used below also appears in [11, Lemma 3.1]. The longer gap lets us show that certain coefficients vanish exactly, which yields both counting estimates.

Section 2 collects the basic lemmas. Sections 3 and 4 give the gaps and the two counting estimates. We finish the proof in Section 5 and verify sharpness in Section 6.

2. Preliminary lemmas

For n∈ℕ0n\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, let

r⁡(n)=#⁡{(a,b)∈A×B∣a+b=n}.r(n)=\#\{(a,b)\in A\times B\mid a+b=n\}.

For a nonnegative integer XX, also let

T(X)=#{(a,b)∈A×B∣a≤X,b≤X,a+b>X}.T(X)=\#\{(a,b)\in A\times B\mid a\leq X,\ b\leq X,\ a+b>X\}.

Splitting the pairs according to whether their sum exceeds XX gives

(2.1) A⁡(X)​B​(X)=∑n=0Xr⁡(n)+T⁡(X).A(X)B(X)=\sum_{n=0}^{X}r(n)+T(X).

We include the standard counting argument from [9, p. 238]; see also [5, p. 85].

Lemma 2.1.

Suppose that AA and BB are infinite additive complements and that A⁡(x)​B​(x)−xA(x)B(x)-x does not tend to +∞+\infty. There is an integer n0≥1n_{0}\geq 1 such that

(2.2) r⁡(n)=1(n≥n0).r(n)=1\qquad(n\geq n_{0}).

There is also a strictly increasing sequence of integers XjX_{j} tending to infinity such that

(2.3) A⁡(Xj)​B​(Xj)=Xj+O⁡(1),T⁡(Xj)=O⁡(1).A(X_{j})B(X_{j})=X_{j}+O(1),\qquad T(X_{j})=O(1).
Proof.

Choose N≥1N\geq 1 such that r⁡(n)≥1r(n)\geq 1 for n≥Nn\geq N. The excess is bounded below. Since it does not tend to infinity, it is bounded above along some sequence tending to infinity. Taking integer parts and then a subsequence gives strictly increasing integers XjX_{j} with A⁡(Xj)​B​(Xj)=Xj+O⁡(1)A(X_{j})B(X_{j})=X_{j}+O(1).

For every integer X≥NX\geq N, (2.1) gives

A⁡(X)​B​(X)−X≥1−N+∑n=NX(r⁡(n)−1).A(X)B(X)-X\geq 1-N+\sum_{n=N}^{X}\bigl(r(n)-1\bigr).

The sum has nonnegative integer terms and is bounded along XjX_{j}. Its partial sums are nondecreasing, so only finitely many terms are nonzero. This proves (2.2) for some n0n_{0}. It follows that ∑n=0Xr⁡(n)=X+O⁡(1)\sum_{n=0}^{X}r(n)=X+O(1), and (2.1) then gives T⁡(Xj)=O⁡(1)T(X_{j})=O(1). ∎

We also need a bound on the number of representations of a difference. For n≥0n\geq 0, define

dA,B​(n)\displaystyle d_{A,B}(n) =#⁡{(a,b)∈A×B∣a−b=n},\displaystyle=\#\{(a,b)\in A\times B\mid a-b=n\},
dB,A​(n)\displaystyle d_{B,A}(n) =#⁡{(a,b)∈A×B∣b−a=n}.\displaystyle=\#\{(a,b)\in A\times B\mid b-a=n\}.
Lemma 2.2.

Suppose that r⁡(n)=1r(n)=1 for every n≥n0n\geq n_{0}. If two distinct pairs satisfy

b−a=b′−a′,(a,b),(a′,b′)∈A×B,b-a=b^{\prime}-a^{\prime},\qquad(a,b),(a^{\prime},b^{\prime})\in A\times B,

then a,a′,b,b′<n0a,a^{\prime},b,b^{\prime}<n_{0}. In particular,

(2.4) dA,B(n)≤1,dB,A(n)≤1(n≥n0).d_{A,B}(n)\leq 1,\qquad d_{B,A}(n)\leq 1\qquad(n\geq n_{0}).
Proof.

The equality of differences gives a+b′=a′+ba+b^{\prime}=a^{\prime}+b. Distinct pairs have a≠a′a\neq a^{\prime} and b≠b′b\neq b^{\prime}, so these are two distinct representations of a sum. By eventual uniqueness, their common value is less than n0n_{0}. Nonnegativity gives a,a′,b,b′<n0a,a^{\prime},b,b^{\prime}<n_{0}, and hence |b−a|<n0|b-a|<n_{0}. This proves both inequalities in (2.4). ∎

To keep track of the finitely many exceptions in (2.2), put

(2.5) δ⁡(n)=r⁡(n)−1(n≥0),E=∑n=0n0−1|δ⁡(n)|,C=E+n0.\delta(n)=r(n)-1\quad(n\geq 0),\qquad E=\sum_{n=0}^{n_{0}-1}|\delta(n)|,\qquad C=E+n_{0}.

Thus δ\delta is supported on [0,n0−1][0,n_{0}-1], and for every integer N≥n0−1N\geq n_{0}-1,

(2.6) ∑n=0Nr⁡(n)=N+1+c,c=∑n=0n0−1δ⁡(n),|c|≤E.\sum_{n=0}^{N}r(n)=N+1+c,\qquad c=\sum_{n=0}^{n_{0}-1}\delta(n),\qquad|c|\leq E.

The constants EE, CC and cc depend only on the values of r⁡(n)r(n) below n0n_{0}, so they do not depend on the gaps chosen later.

For later use, write 𝟏S\mathbf{1}_{S} for the indicator of a set S⊆ℕ0S\subseteq\mathbb{N}_{0}. All functions are extended by zero to negative integers. Their convolution is

(u∗v)​(n)=∑j=0nu⁡(j)​v​(n−j)(n≥0).(u*v)(n)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}u(j)v(n-j)\qquad(n\geq 0).

Convolution is commutative and associative, and convolution with h=𝟏ℕ0h=\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{N}_{0}} gives partial sums.

3. Long gaps from bounded excess

We first find an empty upper half of an initial segment, as in [11, Section 4]. A second comparison, at Xj−xjX_{j}-x_{j}, gives a gap extending beyond 3​xj3x_{j}.

Lemma 3.1.

Suppose that the assumptions of Lemma 2.1 hold. Assume in addition that there is a constant κ\kappa with 1<κ<3/21<\kappa<3/2 such that

(3.1) A⁡(t)​B​(t)≤κ​tfor all sufficiently large real ​t.A(t)B(t)\leq\kappa t\qquad\text{for all sufficiently large real }t.

Fix n0n_{0} as in (2.2). After interchanging AA and BB if necessary, there are consecutive elements xj<yjx_{j}<y_{j} of AA such that xj→∞x_{j}\to\infty and

(3.2) xj≥2​n0,yj≥3​xj+n0.x_{j}\geq 2n_{0},\qquad y_{j}\geq 3x_{j}+n_{0}.
Proof.

Take XjX_{j} from Lemma 2.1. Since A⁡(Xj)​B​(Xj)=Xj+O⁡(1)A(X_{j})B(X_{j})=X_{j}+O(1) and both counting functions tend to infinity,

(3.3) A⁡(Xj)=o⁡(Xj),B⁡(Xj)=o⁡(Xj).A(X_{j})=o(X_{j}),\qquad B(X_{j})=o(X_{j}).

Let

uj=A⁡(Xj)−A⁡(Xj/2),vj=B⁡(Xj)−B⁡(Xj/2).u_{j}=A(X_{j})-A(X_{j}/2),\qquad v_{j}=B(X_{j})-B(X_{j}/2).

Pairs with both elements greater than Xj/2X_{j}/2 are counted by T⁡(Xj)T(X_{j}), so

(3.4) uj​vj≤T⁡(Xj)=O⁡(1).u_{j}v_{j}\leq T(X_{j})=O(1).

If both uju_{j} and vjv_{j} were positive for infinitely many jj, they would both be bounded on that subsequence. Hence

A⁡(Xj/2)​B​(Xj/2)\displaystyle A(X_{j}/2)B(X_{j}/2) =(A⁡(Xj)−uj)​(B⁡(Xj)−vj)\displaystyle=(A(X_{j})-u_{j})(B(X_{j})-v_{j})
=Xj+O⁡(A⁡(Xj)+B⁡(Xj)+1)=Xj+o⁡(Xj).\displaystyle=X_{j}+O(A(X_{j})+B(X_{j})+1)=X_{j}+o(X_{j}).

This contradicts (3.1) at Xj/2X_{j}/2, since κ<2\kappa<2.

Thus at least one of uj,vju_{j},v_{j} is zero for all large jj. After interchanging the sets and passing to a subsequence, we may assume that A∩(Xj/2,Xj]=∅A\cap(X_{j}/2,X_{j}]=\varnothing. Put xj=max⁡(A∩[0,Xj])x_{j}=\max(A\cap[0,X_{j}]). Then xj→∞x_{j}\to\infty and

(3.5) xj≤Xj/2,A∩(xj,Xj]=∅.x_{j}\leq X_{j}/2,\qquad A\cap(x_{j},X_{j}]=\varnothing.

We now compare the counting functions at Xj−xjX_{j}-x_{j}. Every b∈B∩(Xj−xj,Xj]b\in B\cap(X_{j}-x_{j},X_{j}] gives a pair (xj,b)(x_{j},b) counted by T⁡(Xj)T(X_{j}), so

0≤B⁡(Xj)−B⁡(Xj−xj)≤T⁡(Xj)=O⁡(1).0\leq B(X_{j})-B(X_{j}-x_{j})\leq T(X_{j})=O(1).

Also A⁡(Xj−xj)=A⁡(Xj)A(X_{j}-x_{j})=A(X_{j}) by (3.5). Therefore

(3.6) A⁡(Xj−xj)​B​(Xj−xj)=Xj+O⁡(A⁡(Xj)+1)=Xj+o⁡(Xj).A(X_{j}-x_{j})B(X_{j}-x_{j})=X_{j}+O(A(X_{j})+1)=X_{j}+o(X_{j}).

Applying (3.1) at Xj−xjX_{j}-x_{j} gives Xj+o⁡(Xj)≤κ⁡(Xj−xj)X_{j}+o(X_{j})\leq\kappa(X_{j}-x_{j}), or

(3.7) xjXj≤κ−1κ+o⁡(1).\frac{x_{j}}{X_{j}}\leq\frac{\kappa-1}{\kappa}+o(1).

Since (κ−1)/κ<1/3(\kappa-1)/\kappa<1/3, there is a fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0 such that Xj−3​xj≥ε​XjX_{j}-3x_{j}\geq\varepsilon X_{j} for all large jj.

Let yjy_{j} be the next element of AA after xjx_{j}. By (3.5), yj>Xjy_{j}>X_{j}, so yj≥3​xj+n0y_{j}\geq 3x_{j}+n_{0} for large jj. Since xj→∞x_{j}\to\infty, we also have xj≥2​n0x_{j}\geq 2n_{0} eventually. Discarding finitely many terms proves the lemma. ∎

4. Relations between the two counting functions

We first show that the gap in AA forces a gap in BB. This will allow us to estimate both counting functions on [y,y+x][y,y+x].

Lemma 4.1.

Let A,B⊆ℕ0A,B\subseteq\mathbb{N}_{0} satisfy (2.2) for some integer n0≥1n_{0}\geq 1. If x<yx<y are consecutive elements of AA with

x≥2​n0,y≥3​x+n0,x\geq 2n_{0},\qquad y\geq 3x+n_{0},

then

(4.1) B∩[y−x+n0,y+x+n0−1]=∅.B\cap[y-x+n_{0},\ y+x+n_{0}-1]=\varnothing.
Proof.

Put

f=𝟏A∩[0,x],g=𝟏B,h=𝟏ℕ0.f=\mathbf{1}_{A\cap[0,x]},\qquad g=\mathbf{1}_{B},\qquad h=\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{N}_{0}}.

Define the reflected function f~\widetilde{f} by f~​(n)=f​(x−n)\widetilde{f}(n)=f(x-n), and put

D=h−f~∗g.D=h-\widetilde{f}*g.

For n≥0n\geq 0, the coefficient of the convolution is

(4.2) (f~∗g)​(n)=#⁡{(a,b)∈(A∩[0,x])×B∣b−a=n−x}.(\widetilde{f}*g)(n)=\#\{(a,b)\in(A\cap[0,x])\times B\mid b-a=n-x\}.

This follows by writing a=x−ja=x-j and b=n−jb=n-j in the convolution sum. Thus D⁡(n)D(n) is 11 minus the number of these representations of n−xn-x.

Since A∩(x,y)=∅A\cap(x,y)=\varnothing, every representation of an integer below yy uses a≤xa\leq x. Hence f∗g=h+δf*g=h+\delta on [0,y−1][0,y-1]. Using f∗D=f∗h−f~∗(f∗g)f*D=f*h-\widetilde{f}*(f*g), we obtain

(4.3) f∗D=(f−f~)∗h−f~∗δat every index ​0≤n<y.f*D=(f-\widetilde{f})*h-\widetilde{f}*\delta\qquad\text{at every index }0\leq n<y.

Only indices at most nn occur in the substitution, so the identity is valid throughout this range.

For n≥xn\geq x, both (f∗h)​(n)(f*h)(n) and (f~∗h)​(n)(\widetilde{f}*h)(n) equal A⁡(x)A(x). Also, f~\widetilde{f} vanishes outside [0,x][0,x], so (f~∗δ)​(n)=0(\widetilde{f}*\delta)(n)=0 for n≥x+n0n\geq x+n_{0}. It follows from (4.3) that

(4.4) (f∗D)​(n)=0(x+n0≤n<y).(f*D)(n)=0\qquad(x+n_{0}\leq n<y).

To determine where DD vanishes, first note that by Lemma 2.2, a repeated difference can involve only elements less than n0n_{0}. In view of (4.2), this gives

(4.5) D⁡(n)<0⟹x−n0+1≤n≤x+n0−1.D(n)<0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x-n_{0}+1\leq n\leq x+n_{0}-1.

In particular, D⁡(n)≥0D(n)\geq 0 whenever n≥x+n0n\geq x+n_{0}.

Take an integer uu with x+n0≤u≤2​x+n0−1x+n_{0}\leq u\leq 2x+n_{0}-1. The gap hypothesis gives

u+x≤3​x+n0−1<y.u+x\leq 3x+n_{0}-1<y.

Using (4.4) at the index u+xu+x, we obtain

0=(f∗D)​(u+x)=∑a∈Aa≤xD⁡(u+x−a).0=(f*D)(u+x)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a\in A\\ a\leq x\end{subarray}}D(u+x-a).

Every argument is at least x+n0x+n_{0}, so every summand is nonnegative by (4.5). The term with a=xa=x is D⁡(u)D(u), and therefore

(4.6) D⁡(u)=0(x+n0≤u≤2​x+n0−1).D(u)=0\qquad(x+n_{0}\leq u\leq 2x+n_{0}-1).

We claim that the larger interval also satisfies

(4.7) D⁡(n)=0(n0≤n≤2​x+n0−1).D(n)=0\qquad(n_{0}\leq n\leq 2x+n_{0}-1).

Otherwise, choose the largest integer dd in this interval for which D⁡(d)≠0D(d)\neq 0. Relation (4.6) gives d≤x+n0−1d\leq x+n_{0}-1. Consequently,

x+n0≤x+d≤2​x+n0−1<y.x+n_{0}\leq x+d\leq 2x+n_{0}-1<y.

Equation (4.4) at x+dx+d now gives

0=(f∗D)​(x+d)=∑a∈Aa≤xD⁡(x+d−a).0=(f*D)(x+d)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a\in A\\ a\leq x\end{subarray}}D(x+d-a).

For a<xa<x, the argument satisfies

d<x+d−a≤2​x+n0−1.d<x+d-a\leq 2x+n_{0}-1.

All such terms vanish by the choice of dd. The term for a=xa=x is D⁡(d)D(d), which is nonzero. This contradiction proves (4.7).

We can now prove the gap in BB. By (4.2) and (4.7), every integer in

[n0−x,x+n0−1][n_{0}-x,x+n_{0}-1]

has a representation as b′−ab^{\prime}-a with a≤xa\leq x. If bb belonged to the interval in (4.1), then b−yb-y would lie in this interval of differences. Hence

b−y=b′−ab-y=b^{\prime}-a

for some a∈A∩[0,x]a\in A\cap[0,x] and b′∈Bb^{\prime}\in B. The pairs (y,b)(y,b) and (a,b′)(a,b^{\prime}) are distinct, and y≥n0y\geq n_{0}. This contradicts Lemma 2.2 and proves (4.1). ∎

The next lemma uses this gap to control BB and then compares the two segments of AA.

Lemma 4.2.

Under the assumptions of Lemma 4.1, let C=E+n0C=E+n_{0} be as in (2.5). For every integer tt with 0≤t≤x0\leq t\leq x,

(4.8) |A⁡(y+t)−A⁡(x)−A⁡(t)|≤C\lvert A(y+t)-A(x)-A(t)\rvert\leq C

and

(4.9) |A⁡(x)​B​(y+t)−y|≤C.\lvert A(x)B(y+t)-y\rvert\leq C.
Proof.

Put m=A⁡(x)m=A(x). Since x≥2​n0x\geq 2n_{0} and n0≥1n_{0}\geq 1, the gap in (4.1) contains [y,y+x][y,y+x]. Thus

(4.10) B⁡(y+t)=B⁡(y−1)(0≤t≤x).B(y+t)=B(y-1)\qquad(0\leq t\leq x).

Consider the m​B​(y−1)mB(y-1) pairs in

(A∩[0,x])×(B∩[0,y−1]).(A\cap[0,x])\times(B\cap[0,y-1]).

(4.11) y+c=∑n=0y−1r⁡(n)≤m​B​(y−1)≤∑n=0y+n0−1r⁡(n)=y+n0+c.y+c=\sum_{n=0}^{y-1}r(n)\leq mB(y-1)\leq\sum_{n=0}^{y+n_{0}-1}r(n)=y+n_{0}+c.

Since |c|≤E|c|\leq E, equations (4.10) and (4.11) imply (4.9).

It remains to compare the two segments of AA. Put f=𝟏A∩[0,x]f=\mathbf{1}_{A\cap[0,x]}, g=𝟏Bg=\mathbf{1}_{B}, h=𝟏ℕ0h=\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{N}_{0}} and

fy​(n)=𝟏A​(y+n)(n≥0),f_{y}(n)=\mathbf{1}_{A}(y+n)\qquad(n\geq 0),

and extend fyf_{y} by zero to negative integers. For n0≤n≤x+n0−1n_{0}\leq n\leq x+n_{0}-1, consider the unique representation of y+ny+n. If it used an element a≤xa\leq x, then

y−x+n0≤y+n−a≤y+x+n0−1,y-x+n_{0}\leq y+n-a\leq y+x+n_{0}-1,

so the required element of BB would belong to the empty interval (4.1). It must therefore use an element a≥ya\geq y. Thus

(fy∗g)​(n)=1(n0≤n≤x+n0−1).(f_{y}*g)(n)=1\qquad(n_{0}\leq n\leq x+n_{0}-1).

For 0≤n<n00\leq n<n_{0}, the convolution (fy∗g)​(n)(f_{y}*g)(n) is either 00 or 11, since it counts a subset of the representations of y+ny+n, whose representation is unique. Thus there is a function δy\delta_{y}, supported on [0,n0−1][0,n_{0}-1] and taking values in {−1,0}\{-1,0\}, such that

(4.12) fy∗g=h+δyat indices ​0≤n≤x+n0−1.f_{y}*g=h+\delta_{y}\qquad\text{at indices }0\leq n\leq x+n_{0}-1.

The old segment satisfies

5. Proof of Theorem 1.1

Proof.

Suppose that (1.3) holds but (1.2) fails. Choose κ\kappa strictly between 11 and 3/23/2 so that (3.1) holds. Lemmas 2.1 and 3.1 give an integer n0≥1n_{0}\geq 1 satisfying (2.2) and, after interchanging the sets if necessary, consecutive elements xj<yjx_{j}<y_{j} satisfying (3.2).

Fix C=E+n0C=E+n_{0} as in (2.5), and put mj=A⁡(xj)m_{j}=A(x_{j}). Since AA is infinite and xj→∞x_{j}\to\infty, we have mj→∞m_{j}\to\infty. Apply Lemma 4.2 at x=xjx=x_{j}, y=yjy=y_{j}, and t=xjt=x_{j}. Equations (4.8) and (4.9) give

≥(2−Cmj)​(1−Cyj)​yjyj+xj\displaystyle\geq\left(2-\frac{C}{m_{j}}\right)\left(1-\frac{C}{y_{j}}\right)\frac{y_{j}}{y_{j}+x_{j}}
≥34​(2−Cmj)​(1−Cyj).\displaystyle\geq\frac{3}{4}\left(2-\frac{C}{m_{j}}\right)\left(1-\frac{C}{y_{j}}\right).

6. Sharpness

We recall a digit example and verify the endpoint by direct counting. It is a special case of Ma’s construction [7, Lemma 2.1 and equation (3.1)]; the existence of examples at 3/23/2 was proved earlier by Chen and Fang [1].

Let

(6.1) A={∑i≥0εi4i|εi∈{0,1},only finitely many εi≠0},B=2A.A=\left\{\sum_{i\geq 0}\varepsilon_{i}4^{i}\ \middle|\ \varepsilon_{i}\in\{0,1\},\ \text{only finitely many }\varepsilon_{i}\neq 0\right\},\qquad B=2A.

Every base-44 digit is uniquely the sum of a digit in {0,1}\{0,1\} and one in {0,2}\{0,2\}, with no carries. Thus every nonnegative integer has exactly one representation in A+BA+B. At Xk=4k−1X_{k}=4^{k}-1, counting the first kk digits gives

(6.2) A⁡(Xk)=B⁡(Xk)=2k,A⁡(Xk)​B​(Xk)−Xk=1.A(X_{k})=B(X_{k})=2^{k},\qquad A(X_{k})B(X_{k})-X_{k}=1.

To bound the product ratio, write v=∑iεi​2iv=\sum_{i}\varepsilon_{i}2^{i} and put av=∑iεi​4ia_{v}=\sum_{i}\varepsilon_{i}4^{i}. These ava_{v} list AA in increasing order. Since ∑j<iεj​2j≤2i−1\sum_{j<i}\varepsilon_{j}2^{j}\leq 2^{i}-1,

(6.3) v2\displaystyle v^{2} =∑iεi​4i+2​∑iεi​2i​∑j<iεj​2j\displaystyle=\sum_{i}\varepsilon_{i}4^{i}+2\sum_{i}\varepsilon_{i}2^{i}\sum_{j<i}\varepsilon_{j}2^{j}
≤∑iεi​4i+2​∑iεi​2i​(2i−1)≤3​av.\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i}\varepsilon_{i}4^{i}+2\sum_{i}\varepsilon_{i}2^{i}(2^{i}-1)\leq 3a_{v}.

Fix k≥0k\geq 0 and put H=2kH=2^{k}. In [4k,4k+1)[4^{k},4^{k+1}), the elements of AA are 4k+av4^{k}+a_{v}, and those of BB are 2​(4k+av)2(4^{k}+a_{v}), with 0≤v<H0\leq v<H. As av≤(4k−1)/3a_{v}\leq(4^{k}-1)/3, the AA block ends before the BB block begins. Counting at these points gives

A⁡(4k+av)\displaystyle A(4^{k}+a_{v}) =H+v+1,\displaystyle=H+v+1, B⁡(4k+av)\displaystyle B(4^{k}+a_{v}) =H,\displaystyle=H,
A⁡(2​(4k+av))\displaystyle A(2(4^{k}+a_{v})) =2​H,\displaystyle=2H, B⁡(2​(4k+av))\displaystyle B(2(4^{k}+a_{v})) =H+v+1.\displaystyle=H+v+1.

At either point, the product ratio is

H⁡(H+v+1)H2+av≤H⁡(H+v)H2+v2/3+1H≤32+1H,\frac{H(H+v+1)}{H^{2}+a_{v}}\leq\frac{H(H+v)}{H^{2}+v^{2}/3}+\frac{1}{H}\leq\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{H},

where the last inequality follows from

32​(H2+v23)−H⁡(H+v)=(H−v)22≥0.\frac{3}{2}\left(H^{2}+\frac{v^{2}}{3}\right)-H(H+v)=\frac{(H-v)^{2}}{2}\geq 0.

Between consecutive elements of A∪BA\cup B, the numerator is constant and the denominator increases. The same bound therefore holds throughout [4k,4k+1)[4^{k},4^{k+1}), giving

(6.4) lim supx→∞A⁡(x)​B​(x)x≤32.\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{A(x)B(x)}{x}\leq\frac{3}{2}.

For the reverse inequality, take zk=2​(4k−1)/3z_{k}=2(4^{k}-1)/3, the largest element of BB using the first kk digits. Then A⁡(zk)=B⁡(zk)=2kA(z_{k})=B(z_{k})=2^{k}, so

A⁡(zk)​B​(zk)zk=3⋅4k2​(4k−1)⟶32.\frac{A(z_{k})B(z_{k})}{z_{k}}=\frac{3\cdot 4^{k}}{2(4^{k}-1)}\longrightarrow\frac{3}{2}.

Together with (6.2), this proves that the constant 3/23/2 is best possible and that the strict inequality in Theorem 1.1 is necessary.

Acknowledgments and Declaration of AI assistance

When reading Yang and Zhao’s paper, the author believed that the large gap forced another set to emerge with a corresponding gap (their paper only focus on one set), and used ChatGPT to explore the possible relationships. OpenAI Codex was used to assist with literature searches, English editing, the organization of the manuscript, and the checking and revision of some proof details, including the treatment of the finite initial exceptions. The author is responsible for the mathematical arguments, references, and final text.

The author thanks Professor Yang and Professor Zhao for their suggestions. The author expresses his gratitude to his graduate supervisor Huixi Li for his guidance.
